description: We are an interdisciplinary team of students studying biology, applied physics, computer engineering, and cybersecurity. We are passionate about space exploration, science, and technology, and excited to use NASA data to identify Earth locations that resemble the Moon and Mars. Curiosity and teamwork matter most!
summary:
We developed an interactive map-based platform that identifies and explores terrestrial environments that can serve as analogues for potential lunar and Martian locations. The platform brings together 21 candidate sites across Earth—10 Mars analogues and 11 Moon analogues—linking each location to its proposed planetary counterpart.
Users can explore the sites geographically and examine their similarities, including geological features, surface characteristics, environmental conditions, and biological relevance where evidence is available. The platform also presents supporting research and highlights the limitations of each comparison, distinguishing well-established analogues from potential matches that require further investigation.
By organizing scientific evidence in one accessible, interactive resource, our project helps researchers, students, and mission planners explore how Earth environments can inform planetary exploration, analogue testing, and the search for conditions that may support or preserve signs of life beyond Earth.
details:
Project Details

1. Project Overview

We developed an interactive, research-driven planetary analogue mapping platform that connects Earth's diverse geological and environmental landscapes with potential exploration locations on Mars and the Moon.

The project addresses a fundamental challenge in planetary exploration: identifying accessible terrestrial environments that share scientifically relevant characteristics with extraterrestrial landscapes. These environments, known as planetary analogues, provide natural laboratories for investigating geological processes, understanding extreme environmental conditions, studying potential habitability, and preparing technologies and strategies for future robotic and human exploration missions.

Our platform brings together 21 candidate terrestrial analogue locations: 10 proposed Mars analogues and 11 proposed lunar analogues, distributed across different geographical regions and environmental settings.

By combining NASA Earth-observation and climate resources, planetary mission data, scientific literature, and interactive geographical mapping, we transformed dispersed research information into a centralized digital platform. Users can explore candidate locations, examine their proposed planetary counterparts, and understand the scientific characteristics that make each comparison relevant.

Our approach recognizes that no terrestrial environment perfectly reproduces the conditions of Mars or the Moon. Instead, we focus on identifying specific geological, mineralogical, geomorphological, and environmental similarities while acknowledging the differences and limitations of each proposed analogue.

2. How the Platform Works

The platform combines geographical visualization, scientific research, and planetary data to organize and present terrestrial analogue candidates.

A. Geographical exploration

The website features an interactive map developed using Leaflet.js. It displays the selected terrestrial analogue locations and allows users to explore their geographical distribution.

Each candidate location is associated with its geographical coordinates and a proposed lunar or Martian counterpart. This creates a geographical connection between Earth environments and the planetary locations they may help scientists investigate.

B. Earth and planetary data utilization

The research process draws on multiple NASA and USGS data resources to investigate both sides of the Earth-to-planet comparison.

Earth observation and environmental characterization

  • NASA POWER (Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources): Used to obtain climate and environmental information relevant to terrestrial analogue locations. These data provide environmental context for comparing candidate sites and investigating conditions such as meteorological and solar characteristics.
  • NASA/USGS Landsat imagery: Used to examine Earth's surface through satellite observations, supporting the investigation of geographical context, surface patterns, and landscape characteristics relevant to the proposed analogues.

Planetary data and target characterization

  • NASA Planetary Data System (PDS): Consulted for planetary mission data and scientific information relevant to the geological and surface characteristics of lunar and Martian target locations.
  • Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) data resources: Used to investigate lunar geological context and support comparisons between selected terrestrial environments and lunar terrain.

These resources provide complementary perspectives: Earth-observation data help characterize terrestrial environments, while planetary mission data help establish the characteristics of the extraterrestrial locations being compared.

The resulting information was considered alongside scientific publications and incorporated into the structured location database used by the website.

C. Research-based location profiles

The platform's database organizes information for each candidate location, including:

  • Location name and country.
  • Geographical coordinates.
  • Proposed planetary counterpart and its coordinates.
  • Relevant geological and geomorphological features.
  • Environmental characteristics.
  • Mineralogical information where available.
  • Biological and astrobiological findings where relevant.
  • Scientific references supporting the comparison.
  • Limitations and differences between the terrestrial and planetary environments.

This structure allows users to explore not only where an analogue is located, but also why it was selected and what makes it scientifically useful.

3. Scientific Methodology and Analogue Selection

Our approach combines satellite-based observations, planetary data resources, and scientific literature to identify and characterize potential terrestrial analogues.

Rather than selecting locations based exclusively on visual resemblance, we considered several scientific dimensions.

Geological and geomorphological similarity

We investigated geological formations and surface processes relevant to planetary exploration, including:

  • Volcanic fields and basaltic formations.
  • Lava tubes, caves, and subsurface structures.
  • Sedimentary basins and layered geological deposits.
  • Wind-shaped landforms and aeolian processes.
  • Erosion, surface weathering, and exposed geological structures.
  • Polar and periglacial landscapes.

Mineralogical characteristics

Mineral composition can provide important information about the processes that shaped planetary surfaces.

We considered relevant terrestrial formations and deposits, including iron oxides, sulfates, carbonates, silica-rich deposits, evaporites, and basaltic materials.

These characteristics are particularly important when investigating environments associated with past water activity, volcanic processes, sediment deposition, and potential preservation of biosignatures.

Environmental conditions

We considered environmental factors that influence the relevance of a terrestrial analogue, such as:

  • Temperature extremes and temperature variability.
  • Aridity and water availability.
  • Salinity and acidity.
  • Solar exposure and radiation-related environmental stresses.
  • Permafrost and cold-desert conditions.
  • Atmospheric and surface-environment differences.

NASA POWER data and Landsat observations contribute to the terrestrial environmental and surface characterization, while planetary mission data provide context for the target environments.

Scientific evidence and limitations

Each proposed comparison was considered in relation to the scientific evidence available.

We distinguish between established analogues, promising candidate environments, and comparisons that are useful only for particular geological or environmental characteristics.

A location may be relevant for one research question without reproducing the complete geological history or environmental conditions of its planetary counterpart. We therefore include limitations to avoid treating similarity as equivalence.

4. Astrobiological Dimension

An important scientific component of the project is its astrobiological perspective, particularly for the proposed Martian analogues.

Mars is a major target in the search for evidence of past habitability and potential biosignatures. Terrestrial extreme environments provide opportunities to investigate how microorganisms survive environmental stress and how biological signatures may interact with minerals and sediments.

Our research considered several biological and astrobiological themes:

Extremophile survival: Investigating microorganisms adapted to extreme environmental conditions, including xerophiles in extremely dry environments and halophiles in high-salinity environments.

Endolithic and cryptoendolithic microorganisms: Examining microbial communities that inhabit rocks or protected spaces within them, where geological structures may provide protection from environmental stress.

Hydrothermal and mineral-associated microbial systems: Investigating relationships between microbial activity, mineral precipitation, and geological processes in extreme terrestrial environments.

Biosignature preservation: Considering how microbial structures and biological traces may become associated with minerals and sediments, and how such materials can preserve evidence of past biological activity.

Locations such as the Atacama Desert, Lake Salda, El Tatio, Río Tinto, and the McMurdo Dry Valleys provide different research perspectives on microbial adaptation, mineral–microbe interactions, and extreme environmental conditions.

We also distinguish between direct biological evidence documented at a particular location, evidence from its surrounding region, and potential astrobiological relevance inferred from environmental characteristics.

The identification of terrestrial microorganisms does not establish the presence of life on Mars. Instead, these environments help researchers understand the limits of terrestrial life and investigate processes that may be relevant when interpreting extraterrestrial environments.

5. Candidate Locations

The platform currently includes 21 candidate terrestrial analogue locations.

Proposed Mars analogues — 16 locations

  • Wadi Rum — Jordan (Sandstone Desert)
  • Utah Desert — United States (Arid Sedimentary Terrain)
  • Dasht-e Lut — Iran (Yardang & Hyper-Arid Desert)
  • Haughton Crater — Canada (Impact Crater / Arctic)
  • Atacama Desert — Chile (Hyper-Arid Desert)
  • Jiddat al Harasis — Oman (Rocky Desert Plateau)
  • White Desert — Egypt (Eroded Desert Landforms)
  • Harrat ash-Sham — Jordan (Basaltic Volcanic Field)
  • Fagradalsfjall — Iceland (Young Volcanic Terrain)
  • McMurdo Dry Valleys — Antarctica (Polar Cold Desert)

These locations represent different environmental and geological characteristics relevant to Mars, including hyper-aridity, iron-rich surfaces, sedimentary formations, volcanic landscapes, hydrothermal systems, evaporite environments, wind-shaped landforms, and polar conditions.

Proposed lunar analogues — 9 locations

  • Lava Beds — United States (Lava Tube Complex)
  • Ape Cave — United States (Basaltic Lava Tube)
  • Surtshellir — Iceland (Collapsed Lava Tube Roof)
  • Jingpo Lake Volcanic Field — China (Basaltic Flows & Cave Features)
  • Umm Jirsan — Saudi Arabia (Lava Tube with Collapse Openings)
  • Haikou Volcanic Field — China (Basaltic Volcanic Cluster)
  • Fagradalsfjall — Iceland (Young Volcanic Terrain)
  • Harrat ash-Sham — Jordan (Basaltic Volcanic Field)
  • Askja Volcanic Field — Iceland (Caldera & Young Lava Terrain)
  • McMurdo Dry Valleys — Antarctica (Polar Cold Desert)
  • Haughton Crater — Canada (Impact Crater / Arctic)

These locations were selected primarily for their geological and physical relevance to lunar terrain, including basaltic formations, volcanic landscapes, lava tubes, subsurface structures, and environmental and operational challenges associated with planetary exploration.

6. Benefits and Intended Impact

The platform aims to make planetary analogue research more accessible, organized, and useful by connecting geographical information with scientific evidence.

Its main benefits include:

Centralized analogue information: Bringing together geographically distributed locations, environmental observations, planetary references, and scientific publications in one resource.

Accessible geographical exploration: Allowing users to explore terrestrial candidates through an interactive map instead of relying on disconnected lists and research documents.

Data-informed comparisons: Combining Earth-observation and environmental data with planetary mission resources to support more meaningful Earth-to-planet comparisons.

Astrobiological research support: Helping users identify terrestrial environments relevant to microbial adaptation, extreme habitability, and the preservation of potential biosignatures.

Scientific transparency: Presenting the reasoning and limitations behind proposed analogues rather than treating visual similarity as proof of environmental equivalence.

Interdisciplinary collaboration: Connecting planetary science, geology, environmental science, biology, astrobiology, physics, and software development through a shared platform.

Potential users include planetary scientists, astrobiologists, researchers, university students, educators, and teams developing future planetary exploration concepts.

In the longer term, the project could support the identification of locations for terrestrial analogue field studies, exploration technology testing, educational activities, and interdisciplinary research.

7. Creativity and Innovation

The project's main innovation lies in combining NASA and USGS Earth-observation resources, planetary mission information, scientific literature, and geographical exploration into a single interactive platform.

Rather than presenting terrestrial analogues as isolated examples, we connect each candidate to a proposed planetary counterpart and organize the scientific information supporting that comparison.

The platform also recognizes that analogue relevance is multidimensional. A location may be valuable because of its geological structure, another because of its environmental extremes, and another because of its potential to help investigate microbial survival or biosignature preservation.

For example, a terrestrial lava tube may provide a useful geological and structural comparison for lunar subsurface exploration, even though its atmosphere, gravity, temperature, and weathering conditions differ substantially from those of the Moon.

Similarly, a hyper-arid desert can help investigate the limits of microbial survival under severe water limitation without reproducing the complete environmental conditions of Mars.

By presenting these distinctions, the project moves beyond simple visual matching and encourages users to evaluate analogue environments according to their specific scientific relevance.

8. Development Tools and Technologies

The project was developed as a web-based application through collaboration between the team's scientific research and engineering components.

Web development

  • HTML: Used to structure the website's content and interface.
  • CSS: Used to define the visual presentation and layout.
  • JavaScript: Used to implement interactive website functionality.
  • Leaflet.js: Used to develop the interactive geographical map and visualize terrestrial analogue locations.

Scientific and geographical data

  • NASA POWER: Climate and environmental data for terrestrial location characterization.
  • NASA/USGS Landsat: Satellite imagery for Earth-surface observation.
  • NASA Planetary Data System (PDS): Planetary mission data resources and scientific references.
  • Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO): Lunar data resources supporting geological comparisons.

Deployment and hosting

  • Vercel: Used to deploy and host the web application, making the platform accessible online.

AI-assisted development and research

  • Gemini and ChatGPT: Used as research and development assistants.

AI tools supported the development process but were not treated as substitutes for NASA datasets or scientific publications.

9. Interdisciplinary Teamwork

Our five-member team combines academic backgrounds in biotechnology and applied biological sciences, cybersecurity, applied physics, and computer engineering.

This interdisciplinary structure allowed us to address the challenge from complementary perspectives.

The biological sciences background contributed to the investigation of extreme-environment microorganisms and astrobiological relevance. Applied physics contributed to considering planetary and environmental conditions. Computer engineering and network engineering contributed to the development and technical implementation of the web platform.

The result is a project that connects scientific research with software development and geographical data visualization.

10. Future Development

The current platform establishes a foundation for a more comprehensive planetary analogue database.

Future development could introduce:

  • Additional terrestrial analogue locations and planetary targets.
  • Search and filtering by geological, mineralogical, and environmental characteristics.
  • More detailed satellite imagery and remote-sensing layers.
  • Standardized comparison criteria for evaluating analogue relevance.
  • Expanded climate and environmental data visualization.
  • More detailed integration of planetary mission datasets.
  • Tools for comparing multiple candidate locations according to specific research objectives.

These additions could help transform the current platform into a broader resource for planetary analogue discovery, comparative research, and exploration planning.

Conclusion

Our project brings together Earth-observation data, planetary mission resources, scientific literature, and interactive mapping to make terrestrial planetary analogue research easier to explore and understand.

By connecting 21 candidate Earth environments with proposed lunar and Martian counterparts, the platform provides a starting point for investigating the geological, environmental, and biological questions that are important to future planetary exploration.

Earth is more than the place from which we explore other worlds. Its deserts, volcanic landscapes, polar regions, and extreme environments can also serve as natural laboratories for understanding them.
